key_finding: Synthesizes recent DC plan design literature: automatic enrollment and default investments raise participation but can suppress participant engagement, with mixed longer-term effects.
methodology: Narrative state-of-the-art overview of academic and policy literature on DC plan design; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Useful map of the employer-retirement default literature and its engagement caveats, but the mechanism (employer as trusted intermediary) is exactly what the brief says does not transfer, so it should not directly drive the entry-design decision.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
review gives no independent effect sizes
relevance_reason: Broad, recent overview of the default-effect literature that frames the trade-offs the brief is asking about, even though the setting is employer plans.

key_finding: Steady-state saving rate increases from automatic enrollment (0.6% of income) and auto-escalation (0.3%) are much smaller than headline enrollment-rate effects once job turnover, withdrawal on separation, and opt-out from escalation are accounted for.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating turnover, vesting, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: Directly substantiates the support team's objection: nominal enrollment lift overstates the real, persistent increase in saving once attrition and opt-out are modeled, which should temper how much weight the team puts on an enrollment-only metric.
limitations: 401(k) employer retirement plans, not a liquid consumer savings app
abstract does not report round-up/small-sum contexts
relevance_reason: The clearest quantified rebuttal to 'defaults reliably raise saving,' directly relevant to the persistence question (C2) the brief foregrounds.

key_finding: A field experiment shrouding a minimum-payment autopay default cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged users anchored autopay amounts just above the minimum and manual payments fell.
methodology: Randomized field experiment on live credit card accounts with 6-month follow-up on payment behavior and debt outcomes.
why_it_matters: Shows a behavioral nudge in a real consumer financial product can shift the metric it targets (autopay enrollment) while leaving the substantive outcome (debt/amount) unchanged or even producing side effects (missed payments) — a direct warning against equating enrollment with the amount actually saved.
limitations: debt paydown, not savings accumulation
cardholders with liquidity constraints may not generalize to round-up savers
relevance_reason: Consumer fintech field RCT showing enrollment shifts can be decoupled from the outcome that matters (amount), squarely testing the brief's 'vanity metric' concern.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment for low-income employees into the public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most people who could opt out did so, and the default effect was stronger where incentives were high and knowledge of enrollment status was low.
methodology: Natural experiment using nationwide policy rollout, administrative and survey data linkage.
why_it_matters: A large, recent, well-identified default effect size with heterogeneity by knowledge and incentive strength — useful benchmark for the magnitude of an opt-out effect, and a caution that defaults work less well when the choice is simple and easy to reverse (as ours would be).
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system rather than a consumer app
low-income employee population differs from general banking-app users
relevance_reason: Recent, well-identified default effect size with distributional heterogeneity, useful analogy despite pension setting.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to participation and contributions seen at 12 months is substantially attenuated by 36 months, though it still reduces inequality in savings; a life-cycle model fits the pattern with a switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Panel data from over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel; structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly answers the brief's persistence question with a horizon comparison (12 vs 36 months), showing gains shrink over time even though distributional benefits (lower inequality) persist — informs what to measure and when.
limitations: retirement plan savings, not liquid round-up savings
structural model estimates are model-dependent
relevance_reason: Gives an explicit horizon-based attenuation estimate for default effects, central to the brief's 6-12 month persistence question.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term retirement plan participation but induces passivity (low contribution rates, non-management, account churn), so participation alone does not establish welfare improvement.
methodology: Narrative review of empirical literature on default enrollment welfare effects.
why_it_matters: Articulates precisely the trade-off the brief poses (enrollment vs genuine engagement/welfare) and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, reminders) that could be adapted to a round-up multiplier design.
limitations: U.S. retirement system framing
no original data, synthesis only
relevance_reason: Directly frames the enrollment-vs-passivity trade-off central to the brief, though set in retirement plans.

key_finding: Across three experiments (including a 5-country, n=4207 study), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes, but implementing a default — especially one people refuse — lowers users' rating of the advice and perceived honesty of the provider; framing of the default question also shifts amounts invested.
methodology: Multi-study experimental design with a large representative multi-country European sample; manipulates default presence and framing.
why_it_matters: Gives quantitative evidence that a pre-set level can anchor the amount chosen (C3) and that defaults carry a real reputational/trust cost when refused — directly informs whether a pre-set multiplier risks reading as manipulative in the EU market this app operates in.
limitations: financial advice/wealth management context, not a round-up savings app specifically
no long-term follow-up on retention
relevance_reason: European, consumer-facing experimental evidence on both anchoring by presets and the perceived-manipulation cost of defaults — matches two of the brief's core questions.

key_finding: With automatic 401(k) enrollment, participation exceeded 85%, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did so after three years — the low default rate largely offset the participation gain on average savings.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking 401(k) participation, default acceptance, and asset accumulation over multiple years.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a pre-set level anchors people at that level for years, which is exactly the anchoring risk the brief asks about for the round-up multiplier — but the magnitude here is retirement-specific.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) context
no year given in metadata, an older foundational study
relevance_reason: The foundational anchoring-on-default-level finding that current literature (including several other shortlisted papers) argues with.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost (84% from their complementarity), and that adding an intermediate preset option (15% alongside 20/25/30%) captures 69% of achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on large-scale transaction data plus an independent stated-preference survey; counterfactual simulation of alternative preset menus.
why_it_matters: The deviation-cost/opt-out-cost framework is a direct method transfer to designing the round-up multiplier menu: it shows how changing which options are preset reshapes chosen levels without changing underlying preferences, which is exactly the anchoring mechanism (C3) the level decision turns on.
limitations: tipping decisions, not savings contributions
no persistence/retention outcome measured
relevance_reason: Explicit structural method for how preset menu options anchor consumer choices, transferable to designing the round-up multiplier menu.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework for downstream (delayed) default effects on consumer behavior, identifying time course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as the key moderators of whether default effects persist or fade.
methodology: Conceptual synthesis and framework paper reviewing consumer-behavior literature on defaults; abstract-only for specifics.
why_it_matters: Gives a structured way to predict and measure whether the round-up default's enrollment effect will persist or decay — directly useful for deciding what to monitor at 6-12 months rather than a single enrollment snapshot.
limitations: theoretical framework, no original effect sizes
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: The only review-level synthesis specifically about when and why default effects persist or fade downstream, matching the brief's persistence question.

key_finding: Characterizes when opt-out minimization vs. maximization is asymptotically optimal as a default-design rule, extending to cases with externalities, fees, and designer-chooser disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical/analytical model with numerical simulations verifying asymptotic approximations; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general normative logic for choosing defaults when designer and user interests may not align — relevant background for thinking about which multiplier to pre-select, but too abstract to directly specify a number.
limitations: no named empirical population or product setting
purely theoretical, no applied validation
relevance_reason: General theory of optimal default design that could inform the level decision, though it names no consumer or financial setting.

key_finding: An opt-in liquid short-term savings account at five UK firms saw very low take-up (at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated it), but among those who opted in, 96% still had a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of payroll-deduction short-term savings account introduction across five UK firms, 12-month administrative follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly tests opt-in performance for a liquid, withdraw-anytime savings product much like the round-up feature: shows opt-in produces excellent retention among enrollees but negligible overall enrollment, which is the core trade-off the brief is weighing between opt-in and opt-out.
limitations: employer payroll-mediated enrollment, not a standalone consumer app
small sample of five firms
relevance_reason: Closest real-world analogue to the round-up product (liquid, withdrawable short-term savings) tested under opt-in, directly informing the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: Maps EU laws addressing dark patterns (subscription traps, hidden fees, pre-selected defaults, nagging, drip pricing) and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from regulable manipulation.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building based on EU law and regulatory guidance.
why_it_matters: Provides the specific EU legal framework for judging whether pre-selecting opt-out enrollment or a pre-set multiplier would read as an autonomy-violating dark pattern versus a legitimate default — directly shapes which entry/level design is defensible in this jurisdiction.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, not an empirical behavioral study
does not quantify enrollment or persistence effects
relevance_reason: The EU-specific framework for judging manipulative vs. helpful defaults, central to the brief's stated reputational-risk concern.

key_finding: Default enrollment in Medicare Part D has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug use, and beneficiaries remain passive even when the default option causes substantial losses.
methodology: Two natural experiments plus a randomized assignment of default options; a third natural experiment examines drivers of active choice.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help' premise: passivity persists even when the default is costly, which is the strongest evidence for the support team's worry that passively-enrolled users are not well served.
limitations: health insurance enrollment for Medicare beneficiaries, not a consumer banking app
no data on withdrawal or disengagement from a savings product specifically
relevance_reason: Best evidence that default persistence does not imply good outcomes for the defaulted, informing the enrollment-vs-welfare trade-off.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (vs ~50% at lower defaults reported in prior literature), and many stuck to a rate that was likely suboptimal for them.
methodology: Administrative panel analysis of a single employer's 401(k) plan with an unusually high default rate.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence that a pre-set level anchors people onto a rate that may not match their financial capacity, exactly the anchoring risk the round-up multiplier decision faces.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
no active-choice comparison arm
relevance_reason: Strong anchoring evidence for the preset-level decision (C3), though setting is an employer plan.

key_finding: Switching to automatic enrollment dramatically raised 401(k) participation and caused most enrollees to stick to the default contribution rate and default fund allocation.
methodology: Before/after natural experiment at a single large U.S. corporation using administrative 401(k) records.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a default is read as implicit advice, motivating the concern that our preset multiplier could be interpreted the same way rather than as a neutral option.
limitations: 2001 employer retirement-plan study, pre-dates app-based liquid savings and current EU regulatory climate
no persistence data beyond three years, no consumer setting
relevance_reason: Classic reference the newer literature (including several other shortlisted papers) directly argues with; retained as foundational context.

key_finding: Abstract text was not usable (returned only the word 'Trant'); title indicates four large U.K. field experiments on automating short-term (not retirement) payroll savings.
methodology: abstract-only; title suggests field experiments on payroll-linked short-term savings automation, authored by the Choi/Laibson/Beshears group known for default-effect research.
why_it_matters: If the missing content holds, short-term/liquid savings automation is much closer to our round-up product than retirement defaults, but the abstract gives us nothing to act on yet.
limitations: abstract content is corrupted/missing so findings cannot be verified
payroll-based enrollment still involves an employer intermediary
relevance_reason: Title suggests a close match to short-term consumer savings automation, but content could not be assessed.

key_finding: No abstract available; title indicates a comparison of savings behavior between automatic and voluntary enrollment in a defined contribution retirement plan.
methodology: abstract-only; no content to assess study design.
why_it_matters: Potentially another data point on enrollment-design comparison, but with no abstract there is nothing actionable for the entry-mechanism decision.
limitations: no abstract text available
employer-sponsored DC plan, not consumer product
forthcoming 2026, unpublished results unknown
relevance_reason: Topically on point (auto vs voluntary enrollment) but unusable without abstract content.

key_finding: At-scale U.K. bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts cut unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though consumers still only captured less than half of available savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run by major U.K. retail banks on default enrollment into alert features.
why_it_matters: The closest available analogue to our exact decision: automatic (opt-out) enrollment into a helpful banking feature inside a live consumer app, with quantified financial benefit and evidence that even a good default only captures part of the possible gain.
limitations: measures alert engagement/charge reduction rather than a savings/round-up pot specifically
no explicit persistence data beyond the experiment period
no anchoring-on-preset-level analysis
relevance_reason: A UK consumer-bank automatic-enrollment field experiment with real effect sizes, directly on point for the entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised total saving substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies induced only $0.01 of extra saving per $1 of subsidy because 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by automatic contributions.
methodology: Population-level administrative panel data analysis of Danish retirement savings accounts, decomposing active vs. passive responses.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that passive/default mechanisms move total saved amounts (not just nominal enrollment) far more than active-choice incentives, directly bearing on whether active choice can substitute for opt-out.
limitations: Danish retirement/pension accounts with employer and tax-subsidy structure, not a liquid consumer product
does not measure disengagement or withdrawal, only wealth accumulation
relevance_reason: Central evidence on the active-vs-passive saving mechanism and heterogeneity of who responds, though the setting is retirement wealth not liquid round-up savings.

key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' - a forced-choice design that highlights losses from the non-preferred option - as an alternative to opt-out defaults when automatic enrollment is infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Literature review plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against default/no-default conditions.
why_it_matters: This is the same choice-architecture technique the brief is deciding on (active choice at onboarding); enhanced active choice is a concrete, testable variant that could get most of the enrollment lift while avoiding the opt-out reputational and disengagement risk.
limitations: primary application context is medication adherence, not financial products
abstract gives no quantitative enrollment effect sizes for the financial-savings case
relevance_reason: Directly proposes and tests the active-choice mechanism the brief is weighing as an alternative to opt-out, an explicit method transfer to our entry-mechanism decision.

key_finding: A payment-reminder nudge in a Brazilian financial app cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform, comparing users who did and did not receive reminders, with subgroup analysis by prior overdraft history.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the brief's core distributional worry: a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup, which is the exact risk profile to check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults, in a credit-card rather than savings context
no data on 6-12 month persistence
relevance_reason: Consumer fintech RCT showing heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of an automated intervention - the clearest 'who is hurt' evidence in a directly comparable digital-banking setting.

key_finding: Randomly assigning employees to default enrollment in a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points, an effect equivalent to a 50% savings match, driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among salaried employees in Afghanistan with follow-up interventions isolating mechanisms behind the default effect.
why_it_matters: Gives a mechanistic account (cognitive cost, present bias) for why defaults work, useful for predicting whether an opt-out round-up default would work similarly outside a pension context, and notes defaulted savers became more likely to actively choose to save afterward - a persistence signal.
limitations: salary-linked account with employer/payroll intermediation in a developing-country labor market, distant from a EU consumer banking app
no data on withdrawal behavior or amounts saved long-term
relevance_reason: Useful mechanism evidence on why default effects occur, relevant by analogy to whether opt-out enrollment would work for round-up savings.

key_finding: A synthesis of household finance evidence covering consumption/saving, borrowing, and payments, and reviewing choice-architecture interventions (product design, defaults, disclosure) that firms and governments use to shape financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative review/handbook chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and behavioral-economics explanations across household finance topics.
why_it_matters: Provides the broader, up-to-date synthesis of choice-architecture effects in consumer (not employer-plan) financial contexts that the brief asks for as a review giving effect-size context across interventions, useful for calibrating expectations on both the entry and level decisions.
limitations: broad review with no single effect size specific to round-up savings or active choice
abstract does not detail persistence or distributional findings in depth
relevance_reason: The review/synthesis candidate matching the brief's explicit request for at least one review giving effect sizes, and framed around consumer rather than employer-plan finance.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years, roughly offsetting gains from higher participation on average asset accumulation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrollment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a default level anchors most people for years, directly warning that whichever multiplier we pre-select could become a de facto ceiling rather than a neutral starting point.
limitations: 2001 employer 401(k) study, well before app-based liquid savings and EU regulation
no measure of withdrawal or disengagement, only contribution/allocation persistence
relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring evidence the more recent papers in this set (e.g., the 12% default study) directly build on and revisit.
